summary: A news story reports that a team led by Dr. Sunita Menon and Dr. James O'Hare used quantum computing to predict weather with unprecedented precision, via a system called Q-ClimatePredict. It extends reliable forecasts from about seven days to a full month, with claimed benefits for disaster preparedness, agriculture, energy, transport and climate policy. The team is also exploring earthquake early-warning and oceanography applications.
one_line: Dr. Sunita Menon and Dr. James O'Hare's team uses quantum computing in Q-ClimatePredict to forecast weather up to a month ahead.
key_facts: As of September 8, 2023, a team of meteorologists and quantum physicists led by Dr. Sunita Menon and Dr. James O'Hare used quantum computers to predict weather patterns with hitherto unattainable precision.
The team works at the Quantum Atmospheric Research Facility (QARF) in Boulder, Colorado.
The quantum weather system is named "Q-ClimatePredict" and runs on the QUBIT-One quantum computer.
Previously, meteorologists struggled to give accurate forecasts beyond a seven-day window; Dr. O'Hare says the system offers outlooks extending to a full month.
Quantum computers manipulate qubits that can exist in multiple states simultaneously, thanks to superposition and entanglement.
Q-ClimatePredict is said to address chaotic systems and the butterfly effect by tracking minor perturbations across the globe that lead to significant weather developments.
Longer forecasts could help agriculture with planting and harvesting decisions and help renewable energy sectors optimize wind and solar use.
Aviation and maritime industries could gain safer route planning and potentially save millions of dollars in fuel costs.
The system can gauge impacts of policy decisions on carbon emissions, deforestation, and urban development with greater accuracy.
Dr. Menon spoke about quantum forecasting at the Climate Adaptation Summit 2024 in Amsterdam, saying it is about "envisioning and constructing a sustainable future."
QARF researchers are exploring earthquake early-warning systems as a possible expansion of their quantum algorithms.
Quantum-assisted oceanography could help conserve marine ecosystems and clarify effects of changing ocean temperatures and acidity.
